Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

</document>
response:
This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot, and in places it reads as a direct answer to it. It has randomisation, output taken from administrative records, actual hours from timesheets, a registered plan, results split by type of work, and exploratory analysis that is clearly labelled as exploratory. The arithmetic checks out:

| Quantity | Check |
|---|---|
| Actual hours, case-processing | 33.0 / 37.9 → −12.9% ✓ |
| Actual hours, counter | 31.2 / 37.6 → −17.0% ✓ |
| Output per actual hour, case-processing | 0.979 / 0.871 → +12.4–12.5% ✓ |
| Output per actual hour, counter | 0.886 / 0.830 → +6.7% ✓ |
| Case-processing gain if measured against scheduled hours | 0.979 / 0.8 → +22% ✓ |
| Per-hour CIs | Consistent with dividing the per-FTE CIs by the hours ratios ✓ |

The main conclusions are mostly well supported. The issues below are about precision and about a few places where the paper doesn't apply its own standards consistently.

## 1. The sick-days measure may have the same denominator problem the paper criticises

The paper corrects the per-hour gain for actual hours, but the −29% fall in sick days is reported per FTE, with no adjustment for reduced exposure.

- If treated staff moved to four days a week (4 × 7.5 h), they had roughly 20% fewer working days on which they could be off sick.
- On that assumption, about two-thirds of the fall is mechanical, and the fall per scheduled day is only about 11% (0.71 / 0.80).
- The paper should say how the rotas were structured (four days, or five shorter days) and report sick days per scheduled day or hour.
- The −29% is also pooled across both strata and has no confidence interval, unlike the other outcomes.

## 2. "More productive per hour" in counter work is mostly queueing, not productivity

In work driven by a queue, fewer staff serving the same demand means less idle time between contacts. So:

- The +6.7% "output per actual hour" largely reflects busier staff, paid for by the public in longer waits and more abandoned calls. It is not evidence that each hour was worked more effectively.
- The Discussion's phrase "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" should be reworded. The paper's broader point, that per-hour and per-employee productivity come apart, is correct and is strengthened by this.

## 3. The counter results may be inflated by customers moving between offices

Randomising by office prevents contamination between colleagues, but not between customers.

- If members of the public can choose an office or phone line, longer waits at treated offices would push demand towards control offices.
- That would lower treated output and raise control output at the same time, so the difference-in-differences estimate would overstate the effect.
- The numbers hint at something like this. Abandonment rising from 6% to 10% explains only about a 4% fall in contacts handled (90/94). The rest of the 11.4% fall needs an explanation: lower demand, displaced demand, or something else.
- The authors should report demand (contacts *offered*) by arm.

## 4. Waiting times and abandoned calls aren't analysed the way the design requires

- Waits (4.2 → 6.9 minutes) and abandonment (6% → 10%) are reported for treated offices only, before and after.
- Without the control offices' figures, these aren't difference-in-differences estimates. If customers shifted between offices (point 3), control waits may have changed too.
- Abandoned calls also aren't among the registered secondary outcomes. That's fine, but it should be flagged as unregistered, as the meetings data are.

## 5. The quality measures can't yet detect problems in case-processing

- **The appeal measure lags.** Appeals take months to resolve, so a nine-month overturn rate mostly reflects decisions from the pre-period or early in the trial. "Quality was unchanged" is premature.
- **Case mix isn't reported.** "Cases closed" can be held up by clearing easier cases first while harder ones age. The paper reports waiting time for counters but not backlog size, case age, or time-to-decision for case-processing. Those are the natural equivalents and the main risk the limitations section names.
- **Table 1 rows are ambiguous.** "3.1% v 3.0%" and "11.8% v 10.9%" don't say whether the comparison is treated vs control or pre vs post. They have no CIs. The rise in repeat contacts in counter offices isn't discussed.

## 6. Overtime has cost implications the paper doesn't analyse

- Case-processing hours fell by only 13% because of *claimed overtime*. That is paid, possibly at premium rates, on top of unchanged salaries.
- With output per FTE at −2.1% and higher pay costs, cost per case rose. The county's question was about extending the schedule "without loss of service", and cost is the obvious next question. A simple cost-per-output table would help.
- Timesheets capture only *claimed* overtime. Unclaimed extra work would mean actual hours are overstated as having fallen, and the per-hour gain overstated. This is the same bias the paper corrects for scheduled hours, to a smaller degree.

## 7. The confidence intervals may be too narrow

- Clustered standard errors with 10 clusters (counter) or 14 (case-processing) are known to be anti-conservative. The intervals are probably too narrow, especially in the counter stratum.
- Wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference would be more defensible, and both are easy to run with this design.

Related reporting gaps:
- **Test of the difference between strata.** The headline is that the effect "differed sharply by type of work", but the difference between strata isn't formally tested. It is probably significant (about −9 percentage points), but it should be shown.
- **Pooled estimate.** The registered primary outcome has no pooled estimate. If the plan specified results by stratum, say so. If not, report the pooled figure.
- **Baseline balance.** There is no table comparing the arms at baseline, which matters with 5 or 7 offices per arm.
- **"Little or no measurable loss".** A CI running to −6.8% includes a meaningful loss, so this phrase is generous. Without a prespecified equivalence margin, "no statistically significant loss; a loss of up to about 7% cannot be ruled out" is more accurate.

## 8. The meetings analysis is well caveated, but the numbers suggest it could be bigger than "part"

The caveats are good. A few additions:

- **No baseline measure.** The 3.3-hour difference comes from month six only. Without pre-period calendar data, it can't be attributed to the treatment rather than to baseline differences between offices.
- **Very wide uncertainty.** With n = 7, r = 0.71 has a 95% CI of roughly −0.05 to 0.95.
- **Possible size of the effect.** A rough illustrative calculation, assuming similar meeting time at baseline:
  - Non-meeting hours were about 29.2 per week in treated offices (33.0 − 3.8) and about 30.8 in control offices (37.9 − 7.1). That is only about 5% fewer working hours outside meetings.
  - Output per non-meeting hour would then be up only about 3% (0.979 / 0.948).
  - So cutting meetings could plausibly account for *most* of the 12.5%, not just part of it. That strengthens the case for the registered confirmatory test.

## 9. Minor points

- The Summary is otherwise careful, but it reports the counter per-hour gain without its CI and leaves out abandoned calls. Abandonment is arguably the most important service outcome for the public.
- It would help to report what the counter results would look like against scheduled hours (+10.8%). That supports the paper's third conclusion across both strata.
- On external validity: treated counter offices kept opening hours and staffing unchanged. The result answers "cut hours without backfilling". It says nothing about cutting hours while hiring to cover, which is the policy option most employers would actually face.

## Overall

The central claims hold:
- In backlog work, output per employee was roughly maintained.
- In coverage work, it fell and service worsened.
- Measuring against scheduled hours roughly doubles the apparent gain in output per hour.

The most important fixes are:
1. Report sick days per scheduled day.
2. Report wait and abandonment data for control offices, plus demand offered by arm.
3. Add backlog and case-age measures for case-processing.
4. Use small-cluster inference.
5. Add a short cost analysis.

Set against the Halden paper, this is the right model: it states the limits of its claims and draws them roughly where the evidence puts them.
